title: Historic Cemeteries in Natchez MS – A Walking Guide
h1: Explore Natchez’s Historic Cemeteries on Foot
meta_description: Discover Natchez's historic cemeteries with our walking guide. Learn routes, stories, and tips for a memorable stroll through the city’s past.
intro: Imagine stepping out of downtown Natchez on a warm Saturday morning, coffee in hand, and letting the city’s history guide your feet. The streets you’ve walked a hundred times—Canal, Main, the bluff‑side road that hugs the Mississippi—hold more than storefronts; they border quiet, moss‑draped cemeteries where the past still whispers. In this guide we’ll wander past the grand marble of Natchez City Cemetery, slip through the overgrown lanes of St. Peter’s, linger at the solemn Confederate Memorial, and finish at the hidden gems tucked behind St. Mary's. You’ll get a sense of each site’s story, practical tips for navigating the grounds, and a few local quirks that only longtime residents notice. Ready to lace up your walking shoes and let the dead do the talking?

sections.heading: Natchez City Cemetery: Grand Vistas and Family Legends
sections.body: Natchez City Cemetery sits just a block off Canal Street, a short stroll from the river bluff where the wind carries the scent of magnolia. As you cross the wrought‑iron gate, the first thing you notice is the sweeping expanse of oak‑lined avenues that seem to stretch forever. The layout follows a 19th‑century garden‑cemetery model, with winding paths that invite you to wander at a leisurely pace. Look up and you’ll see the towering marble angel of the Sturdivant family, a reminder of the cotton barons who once ruled the town. The cemetery is not just a place of stone; it’s a living archive. You’ll find the grave of Stephen Duncan, a name that still surfaces in local tours, and the modest headstone of a formerly enslaved woman named Mary, whose epitaph reads simply, "Loved by all." The grounds are well‑maintained in spring, with azaleas blooming along the north side, but summer heat can make the stone feel scorching underfoot, so bring water. Parking is limited on the lot behind the Natchez Visitor Center, and the gate closes at dusk, so plan to arrive early if you want the soft morning light that makes the ironwork glow. Don’t miss the small chapel at the far end—it’s a quiet spot for reflection, and the occasional local historian will be there sharing stories about the families interred. While the cemetery is beautiful, it can get crowded during the annual Natchez Pilgrimage, when reenactors and tourists swarm the grounds. If you prefer solitude, aim for a weekday morning in early fall when the leaves are turning and the air is crisp.

sections.heading: St. Peter’s Catholic Cemetery: Hidden History on the Bluff
sections.body: Tucked behind St. Peter’s Church on the hill that looks over the Mississippi, St. Peter’s Catholic Cemetery is the kind of place you might miss if you’re only following the main tourist routes. The narrow, unpaved lane off Liberty Road leads you past a rusted fence and into a world where moss clings to every stone. The cemetery dates back to the 1840s, making it one of the oldest Catholic burial grounds west of the river. Here you’ll find the weathered tomb of Father Jean‑Baptiste LeBlanc, the missionary who first taught French‑speaking settlers to read the Bible in their own tongue. The gravestones are a mix of French‑style obelisks and simple wooden markers, many of which have been replaced with newer marble slabs that still retain the original inscriptions. The most striking feature is a family plot belonging to the Lenoirs, whose ironwork fence is still intact, though the paint has peeled away to reveal a rusted patina that tells its own story. The site is quiet, except for the occasional crow that circles overhead, and the occasional hummingbird that darts near the wildflowers that sprout between the stones. Visiting in late spring, you’ll see purple wild lupines swaying in the breeze, adding a splash of color to the somber surroundings. The cemetery is free to enter, but there is no formal parking; you’ll need to pull onto the side of US‑61 and walk the short distance up the hill. The path can be uneven, so sturdy shoes are advisable. Because it’s less trafficked, you might encounter locals who are maintaining the grounds, sweeping away leaves, or polishing the older stones—a reminder that this place is still cared for by the community. If you’re looking for a more intimate glimpse into Natchez’s multicultural past, St. Peter’s offers a quiet, reflective experience that feels like stepping into a different era.

sections.heading: Confederate Memorial Cemetery: A Contested Landscape
sections.body: The Confederate Memorial Cemetery sits on the outskirts of downtown, just off the intersection of Main Street and US‑61, where the traffic slows enough for you to take a breath and consider the weight of history. Established in 1866, the cemetery was intended as a burial ground for Confederate soldiers who died in nearby hospitals or were brought back from battlefields. The rows of uniform gray headstones are stark, each bearing the same simple inscription: "Soldier of the Confederacy, Died 1863-1865." The centerpiece is a towering granite obelisk, its base surrounded by a low iron fence that has seen better days. Walking among the graves, you can feel the tension between reverence and the modern debate over how we remember this past. The site is maintained by the Natchez Historical Society, which offers occasional guided tours that explain the context of the cemetery, the families involved, and the ongoing discussions about its place in the city’s narrative. It’s not a place for a quick photo op; the solemn atmosphere commands respect, and the occasional tour group can make it feel a bit crowded, especially on Memorial Day weekend. If you decide to visit, aim for early morning on a weekday when the light filters through the towering oaks, casting long shadows that add a contemplative mood. Parking is limited to a small lot behind the cemetery office, so plan to arrive on foot if you’re staying in the downtown area. Bring a notebook if you’re interested in recording the names you encounter—many of the soldiers are linked to local families, and you might discover a connection to your own ancestry. The cemetery is a reminder that Natchez’s history is layered, and walking its grounds offers a chance to confront that complexity head‑on.

sections.heading: St. Mary’s Episcopal Cemetery: Quiet Corners and River Views
sections.body: Just a short walk north of the historic district, past the bustling cafés on Main and the art galleries on Canal, you’ll find St. Mary’s Episcopal Cemetery perched on a gentle rise that overlooks the Mississippi River. The cemetery is accessed through a modest stone gate set back from the church’s front steps, and as you cross the threshold you’re greeted by a sense of calm that feels worlds away from the traffic on US‑61. The layout is informal, with winding paths that lead you past family plots shaded by ancient live oaks draped in Spanish moss. One of the most striking graves is that of William H. McCarty, a riverboat captain whose marble slab bears a carving of a paddlewheel steamer—a nod to the river that shaped Natchez’s fortunes. The cemetery also holds the graves of several African‑American families who were long‑serving caretakers of the church, their modest headstones marked with simple wooden crosses that have been replaced with bronze plaques in recent years. The river view is especially beautiful at sunset; the sky turns pink and gold, reflecting off the water while the silhouettes of the oak trees create a picturesque backdrop. Because the site is less advertised, it rarely feels crowded, making it ideal for a quiet afternoon of contemplation or a gentle stroll after a day of shopping on Main Street. Parking is available on the church’s side lot, but the lot fills up quickly on Sundays when services are held, so a weekday visit is preferable. The cemetery is open daily from dawn to dusk, and you’ll often hear the distant call of riverboats as they pass by. If you’re a photographer, bring a tripod—the low‑light conditions at dusk can produce stunning images of the river’s glow against the historic stonework. St. Mary’s offers a blend of natural beauty and layered history that makes it a perfect finale to your walking tour of Natchez’s historic cemeteries.

faqs.q: Are Natchez historic cemeteries open year round?
faqs.a: Yes, most of Natchez’s historic cemeteries, including Natchez City Cemetery, St. Peter’s Catholic Cemetery, and St. Mary’s Episcopal Cemetery, are open daily from sunrise to sunset. The Confederate Memorial Cemetery has limited hours during winter, closing at 5 p.m. Check the Natchez Historical Society website for any seasonal closures.

faqs.q: Is there an admission fee to visit any of the cemeteries?
faqs.a: All of the cemeteries listed in the guide are free to enter. Some guided tours, especially at the Confederate Memorial Cemetery, may have a small fee of $5–$10 to cover staffing and informational materials.

faqs.q: What’s the best time of day to photograph the gravestones?
faqs.a: Early morning light, roughly an hour after sunrise, gives the stones a warm glow and reduces harsh shadows. Late afternoon, especially at St. Mary’s Episcopal Cemetery, offers dramatic river backdrops as the sun sets behind the Mississippi.

faqs.q: Are pets allowed in Natchez’s historic cemeteries?
faqs.a: Pets are permitted on leashes no longer than six feet. Some cemeteries, like St. Peter’s Catholic Cemetery, ask owners to keep dogs away from fragile headstones to protect the historic markers.

faqs.q: Can I locate a specific ancestor’s grave in these cemeteries?
faqs.a: Yes, most cemeteries maintain searchable online databases through the Natchez Historical Society. You can also call the office of Natchez City Cemetery or St. Mary’s Episcopal Cemetery for assistance; they often provide maps and can point you to the exact plot.
